extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing §101 guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the USPTO's 2014 Interim Guidance two‑part framework to determine whether patent claims are directed to statutory subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, including preparatory steps, the Step 1 statutory category test, Step 2A (directed to a judicial exception), and Step 2B (whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for Analysis – What Has Applicant Invented?
rubrics_metrics.description: Before analyzing for eligibility or any other patentability requirement: review the detailed disclosure and specific embodiments to understand what the applicant has invented; determine the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claims; identify the boundaries of protection sought by applicant; understand how the claims relate to and define what applicant has indicated as the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2103 for more information. Understanding the disclosure and BRI is a prerequisite to proper §101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim when performing the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI governs claim scope for examination; interpret claim language in light of the specification to identify what is recited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the claim as a whole when performing the §101 judicial-exception analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all claim elements individually and in combination; do not isolate a single element absent context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice compact prosecution — examine under other statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice compact prosecution by fully examining under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 103, 112, and 101 (utility, inventorship, and double patenting) and non‑statutory double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when performing a §101 analysis, examiners should continue full examination for other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory Categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter? The claim must be directed to one of the four patent-eligible subject matter categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no, the claim is not eligible and should be rejected as being drawn to non‑statutory subject matter. Use revised form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. See MPEP 2106(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2: Two‑part judicial‑exceptions analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2: A two‑part analysis to determine whether a claim that is directed to a judicial exception recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the exception (used for all claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This replaces prior guidance and should be applied to identify laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas, and then determine whether the claim adds significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: 'Directed to' a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A: Is the claim directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea? 'Directed to' means the exception is recited in the claim, i.e., the claim sets forth or describes the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no, the claim is eligible and examination continues. If yes, proceed to Step 2B. Example: a claim reciting F=ma is directed to an exception. If the claim recites an exception but clearly does not seek to 'tie up' the exception, a streamlined analysis may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of judicial exceptions; no bright line
rubrics_metrics.description: Law of Nature, Natural Phenomenon, Abstract Idea — these are labels courts commonly use but there is no bright line between the exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the exception recited in the claim; the analysis is the same regardless of which label is used. Even narrowly defined exceptions (e.g., highly detailed mathematical formula) will trigger eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of Nature / Natural Phenomena — types and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts that fall under laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles (physical, chemical, biological), naturally occurring substances, and substances that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an isolated DNA; a correlation that is the consequence of how a certain compound is metabolized by the body; electromagnetism to transmit signals; the chemical principle underlying union between fatty elements and water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature‑based products — markedly different characteristics test
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature‑based products are products derived from natural sources that require closer scrutiny: eligible nature‑based products exhibit markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart; nature‑based products that are naturally occurring or not markedly different fall within a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'nature‑based' includes both eligible and ineligible products. See detailed training on analyzing nature‑based products and nature‑based product examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas — types and instruction to identify
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas include: fundamental economic practices; certain methods of organizing human activities; ideas themselves; mathematical relationships/formulas. When making a rejection, specifically identify the abstract idea (e.g., the claim recites the steps of creating a contractual relationship) rather than merely labeling its type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software or business methods are not automatically abstract ideas; identify the specific concept recited in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts' examples of abstract ideas include: mitigating settlement risk; hedging; creating a contractual relationship; using advertising as an exchange; processing information through a clearinghouse; comparing new and stored information using rules; comparing a patient's gene with the wild‑type gene to identify differences; organizing information with categories; mathematical correlations; managing a game of Bingo; Arrhenius equation; formulas for updating alarm limits; converting numerical representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these examples to compare and identify whether a claimed concept maps to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Does the claim as a whole amount to 'significantly more'?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception; analyze each claim as a whole and consider additional elements individually and as an ordered combination to ensure the claim applies the exception in a meaningful way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While this analysis no longer weighs factors, considerations are similar to prior Bilski and Mayo/Myriad guidance. Consider each claim separately; similar claims do not automatically rise or fall together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the additional limitations in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering the claim as a whole, determine whether the additional elements in the claim establish meaningful limitations on the exception and are more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual elements may not add significantly more alone but may do so in combination. Evaluate specific elements recited in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that may qualify as 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that may be enough to qualify as significantly more include: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to the functioning of the computer itself; applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adding a specific limitation other than what is well‑understood, routine and conventional in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the exception to a technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are considerations that support finding 'significantly more' when appropriately recited in claim elements or combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that are not enough to qualify as 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations found not sufficient include: merely adding the words 'apply it' or equivalent instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; simply appending well‑understood, routine and conventional activities known to the industry at a high level of generality; adding insignificant extrasolution activity (e.g., mere data gathering); generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use; using a generic computer to perform generic computer functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a claim requiring only a generic computer to perform generic functions; data gathering steps that are routine; mere recitation of computer implementation does not render an abstract idea patent‑eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome when Step 2B is Yes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception, the claim qualifies as eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility analysis is complete; examiners should continue to examine under other statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. §§ 101 (utility, inventorship, double patenting), 102, 103, 112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome when Step 2B is No
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole does not recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception, the claim is not eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05 [revised] and 7.05.015 [new]; examiners should continue examination under other statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. §§ 101 (utility, inventorship, double patenting), 102, 103, 112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting a plurality of judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites multiple judicial exceptions, conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions; if the claim recites elements that amount to significantly more than that exception, consider whether those elements ensure the claim does not have a preemptive effect for other claimed exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Step 2B: YES for one exception, Step 2B is likely satisfied for all exceptions in the claim; if Step 2B: NO for one exception, then the claim is ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making the §101 rejection — required content
rubrics_metrics.description: The rejection should include identification of the judicial exception by explaining how it is recited in the claim and an explanation of why it is considered an exception; identification of the additional elements in the claim, if any, and an explanation of why they do not add significantly more to the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear, claim‑specific explanation tying claim language to the exception and showing why additional elements are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: New §101 rejections should not be final (when new grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner determines that new grounds of rejection should be made under §101 that are not necessitated by applicant’s amendment of the claims, the Office action should be non‑final so applicant can respond to new grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 706.07(a) regarding appropriate circumstances for making a rejection final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of new form paragraph 7.05.015
rubrics_metrics.description: Use new form paragraph 7.05.015 when rejecting a claim directed to a judicial exception without significantly more. (Provides template rejection language identifying the exception and explaining why additional elements do not amount to significantly more.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form ¶ 7.05.015 text should be used in Office actions; older form paragraphs 7.05.011–7.05.014 should no longer be used and will be deleted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant response to a §101 rejection — acceptable approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper response: persuasive arguments/evidence that the claim is not directed to a judicial exception; persuasive arguments/evidence that additional elements amount to significantly more; or claim amendments (removing/adding/changing elements) that cause the claim to not be directed to the exception or to amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should be given opportunity to present evidence and amendments; examiners should consider such responses in further prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis for claims that do not seek to 'tie up' an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: For efficient examination, a streamlined analysis can be used for claims that clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception — such claims may recite an exception, but eligibility will be self‑evident, so no detailed analysis is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is doubt whether the claim seeks coverage for a judicial exception, perform a full analysis. See provided streamlined examples (hip prosthesis, robotic arm) illustrating when full analysis is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case law examples to apply the framework (e.g., Mayo, Alice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the framework to prior case law facts to illustrate how claims were analyzed under Step 1/Step 2A/Step 2B (e.g., Mayo — law of nature; Alice — abstract idea) and the reasons for eligibility/ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show identifying the exception, assessing additional elements, and concluding whether elements add significantly more (e.g., Mayo: 'administering' and 'determining' were routine data gathering; Alice: recited hardware was generic).
